analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient ratios in every hospital unit and protects nurses who object to unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and then a Health subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital in the country — including VA, military, and Indian Health Service hospitals — to keep enough nurses on each shift that no direct-care registered nurse is responsible for more than a set number of patients, from one patient in trauma and operating rooms to four on a typical medical-surgical floor. It would have let nurses refuse assignments they believe are unsafe without being fired, forced hospitals to post and publicly record actual staffing levels, and set up a hotline and federal enforcement with civil penalties for hospitals that violate the ratios. It also would have added stipends to nursing scholarship programs and expanded grants to recruit and retain nurses.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients get a guaranteed minimum of nursing attention wherever they are treated, with staffing levels posted publicly and a hotline to report violations. Registered and licensed practical nurses get workload limits, a ban on using mandatory overtime to cover the ratios, and legal protection — including the right to sue for reinstatement and back pay — if they are punished for refusing an assignment they believe is unsafe or beyond their training. Nursing students and new graduates benefit from expanded scholarship stipends and retention grants aimed at keeping nurses in bedside care.

how_it_helps.text: It caps how many patients one nurse can be assigned in each hospital unit — from 1 in trauma and operating rooms to 4 on medical-surgical floors and 6 in well-baby nurseries — and forbids hospitals from averaging ratios across a unit or covering gaps with mandatory overtime [S2][S3].

It lets nurses refuse assignments they believe violate the ratios or that they are not trained to handle safely, and bars hospitals from firing, disciplining, or reporting such nurses to state licensing boards; nurses who are retaliated against can sue for reinstatement, back pay, and damages [S3].

It requires hospitals to post actual staffing levels in each unit, keep three years of records open to the public, and submit to federal audits, and it establishes a toll-free hotline patients can use to report inadequate staffing [S2][S3].
It adds stipends to the nurse workforce scholarship and loan repayment program and expands nurse retention grants to fund preceptorship and mentorship projects for new nurses [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals bear the main cost: hiring enough nurses to meet the ratios, keeping three years of staffing records open to public inspection, and civil money penalties up to $25,000 per knowing violation, with higher penalties for repeat offenders. The bill adjusts Medicare payments to cover compliance costs attributable to Medicare patients, but hospitals would absorb the added labor cost for privately insured and uninsured patients, some of which could flow through to premiums and hospital budgets. Federal taxpayers fund the expanded nursing scholarship, retention, and enforcement programs.

drawbacks.text: Hiring enough nurses to meet fixed ratios is expensive, and the bill's Medicare payment adjustment covers only costs attributable to Medicare beneficiaries — hospitals would bear the remaining added cost for privately insured and uninsured patients, some of which could be passed on through insurance premiums or pressure on hospital budgets [S2][S3].

Fixed unit-by-unit ratios are rigid: two ICUs with very different patient mixes would face the same 1-to-2 requirement, and the bill's answer — a national acuity tool developed by HHS within two years — concentrates considerable staffing decisions in one federal process [S3].

Small and rural hospitals, which often already struggle to recruit nurses, would have to comply within four years, and the bill's answer to the resulting shortage — loan repayment stipends and retention grants — is modest relative to the scale of the mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: the bill's own findings cite a Joint Commission report attributing nearly a quarter of unanticipated patient injuries and deaths to understaffing [S3], and fixing an assignment floor addresses both patient safety and the working conditions driving nurses out of bedside care [S3]. The costs are real and the bill only partly covers them: Medicare reimbursement is adjusted only for costs attributable to Medicare beneficiaries [S2], so hospitals would absorb much of the expense for privately insured and uninsured patients, with some of that passed on through insurance premiums and local budgets. Fixed unit-by-unit ratios are also less flexible than a purely acuity-driven system, though the bill layers a national acuity tool on top of the minimums to raise staffing where patients are sicker [S3]. On balance it is a strong patient- and worker-protection bill whose main design weakness is incomplete cost coverage, and it never received the hearing that would have tested those tradeoffs in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then passed down to their Health subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 9, 2013, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S1][S5].
Within two days it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and a second referral to that subcommittee followed in early June; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever appears in the record [S5].
All 38 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals came out ahead: they avoided mandatory nurse-to-patient ratios, public staffing records, and civil penalties, keeping staffing decisions and labor costs under their own control. Nurses and hospital patients gained nothing from the bill's failure.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill also never moved in committees controlled by the Republican majority [S4][S5].

industries.note: Hospitals would have to hire enough registered and licensed practical nurses to meet fixed unit-by-unit ratios, keep detailed public staffing records, and face civil penalties of up to $25,000 per knowing violation [S2][S3]. The bill adjusts Medicare payments to offset compliance costs for Medicare patients, but hospitals would bear the remaining added labor costs for other patients — the main reason the hospital industry has historically opposed staffing ratio mandates.

Nurses gain enforceable workload limits, a prohibition on mandatory overtime to cover the ratios, and legal protection when they refuse assignments they cannot safely perform [S2][S3]. The bill also adds scholarship stipends, preceptorships, and mentorship programs aimed at recruiting and keeping nurses in bedside care [S2].

The bill requires that hospital staffing plans be developed with input from direct-care nurses and their collective bargaining representatives, and bars hospitals from interfering with nurses' rights to organize under the National Labor Relations Act [S3].
